title: What the West should make of Xi’s return to Delhi for the BRICS
gist: Xi arrives in New Delhi with around 400 officials for the first time in seven years, but the author argues reading the Xi-Putin-Modi photograph as India drifting from the West gets India's strategy backwards: New Delhi is 'non-Western, not anti-Western', opposes a BRICS currency, kept the May foreign ministers' failure as a chair's statement rather than imposing a line, and has diversified overwhelmingly toward Western partners.

insights.claim: Xi Jinping is confirmed to arrive in New Delhi for the first time in seven years accompanied by a delegation of around 400 officials, with Putin also present and bilaterals including Iran on the sidelines.
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of realignment headlines off the imagery; the author's view is that this is a fade, not a signal.
insights.locator: China’s President Xi Jinping is now confirmed
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: Interpreting the Xi-Putin-Modi imagery as India drifting away from the West amid Trump's tariff pressure gets India's strategy almost exactly backwards.
insights.so_what: If markets discount Indian-Western alignment on summit optics, that mispricing is the opportunity — the substantive diplomacy points the other way.
insights.quote: Such a reading gets India’s strategy almost exactly backwards.
insights.locator: Images of Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: India positions itself as 'non-Western, not anti-Western' in Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar's formulation — a reformist rather than revisionist power seeking a larger voice, a permanent UNSC seat and influence over financial and technological rulemaking without overturning a system its rise depends on.
insights.so_what: The reformist/revisionist distinction is the right frame for pricing Indian behaviour in any multilateral forum — India defects on voice, not on the system itself.
insights.locator: As Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has put it
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: India's BRICS chairmanship has focused discussions on food security, emerging technologies and trade around strengthening existing institutions rather than replacing them, with BRICS trade ministers calling for the multilateral trading order to be preserved and revitalised amid US tariff volatility.
insights.so_what: BRICS under Indian chairmanship is a status-quo-preserving forum on trade — a counterweight to assumptions that the bloc is building an alternative order.
insights.locator: India’s turn as BRICS chair reflects that approach
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: Beneath BRICS expansion — which India and Brazil both resisted — lies a structural divide: India and Brazil see BRICS as an economic platform while China and Russia treat it as a geopolitical one, and enlargement has made consensus harder.
insights.so_what: The economic-versus-geopolitical split caps what BRICS can deliver; expect declaratory outputs rather than binding mechanisms.
insights.locator: BRICS is also where India’s balancing act faces its toughest test
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: When BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree a joint declaration in May, India as chair issued a chair's statement acknowledging disagreements rather than imposing a common line — the opposite of what a government tilting toward an ideological bloc would do.
insights.so_what: A concrete behavioural test already run and passed: India declined to paper over bloc division, which is evidence against the realignment thesis.
insights.locator: The strain was visible in May
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: India has no interest in leading a financial revolt against the US dollar, opposes a BRICS currency, and instead backs local-currency settlement and easier cross-border payments — seeking resilience and flexibility, not an alternative financial order.
insights.so_what: De-dollarisation headlines out of BRICS lack their second-largest member's support; position sizing on that theme should reflect India's veto.
insights.locator: Debates over de-dollarisation are equally instructive
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

themes.theme: Why the West remains irreplaceable for India

insights.claim: The United States remains India's largest market and a critical source of capital, technology and investment that neither China nor Russia can replace, particularly for semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence.
insights.so_what: India's growth model is structurally tied to Western capital and technology — a hard constraint that bounds how far any China thaw can go.
insights.locator: The United States remains India’s largest market
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: Where India has diversified it has found partners overwhelmingly in the Western camp: the Quad continues streamlining agendas, defence and technology cooperation with the US is expanding despite political headwinds, and trade and defence cooperation with Britain, the EU and Australia has accelerated.
insights.so_what: Revealed preference in actual partnership flows contradicts the drift narrative — track deal announcements rather than summit attendance.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the rest of India’s diplomacy
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: Indian strategists frame the hedge as being against American volatility rather than against America itself, with US tariff pressure, sanctions uncertainty and setbacks to projects such as Chabahar in Iran raising the need for risk management alternatives.
insights.so_what: US policy unpredictability, not US power, is what drives Indian diversification — reducing volatility would slow the hedging, which is a policy lever Washington controls.
insights.quote: India’s hedge is against American volatility, not against America itself
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: Alternatives are not substitutes: India's risk-management diversification does not displace the relationships underpinning its rise.
insights.so_what: A clean rule for reading hedging behaviour anywhere — count whether the new partner can replace the old one's function before calling it realignment.
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: The India-China thaw should not be mistaken for reconciliation: the boundary dispute is unresolved, the trade deficit remains large, dependence on Chinese supply chains is increasingly viewed as a vulnerability, and recent border talks produced language suggesting progress but no breakthroughs.
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate India-China commercial normalisation from diplomatic warmth; supply-chain derisking from China remains Indian policy direction.
insights.locator: The thaw between India and China
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: The Line of Actual Control remains a heavily militarised frontier defined by caution and deterrence, managed through mechanisms that contain tension rather than resolve it.
insights.so_what: Border risk is contained, not removed — a persistent tail risk that resurfaces with any incident regardless of summit atmospherics.
insights.locator: The two sides have built mechanisms
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

themes.theme: The real stake for the West

insights.claim: A BRICS that remains a coalition seeking greater voice for non-Western states is an irritant the West could live with, but a BRICS organised around Chinese preferences would be something else entirely — and India is the most important country capable of preventing that outcome.
insights.so_what: India's continued presence inside BRICS is a Western interest, not a defection — pressuring India out of the bloc would be strategically counterproductive.
insights.quote: A BRICS organised around Chinese preferences would be something else entirely.
insights.locator: A BRICS that remains a coalition
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai

insights.claim: The decisive variable at the summit is whether India can continue holding the line it has spent two decades constructing, not the leaders' photograph.
insights.so_what: Watch the summit's declaration language and whether Chinese framing prevails — that is the measurable outcome, not the optics.
insights.quote: The story this weekend is not the photograph of Xi, Putin and Modi. It is whether India can continue holding the line.
insights.locator: Which is why the story this weekend
insights.speaker: Shruti Pandalai
